case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a plaintiff suing a foreign state under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act must also prove the foreign state has constitutionally sufficient “minimum contacts” with the United States before a federal court may exercise personal jurisdiction.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA), particularly 28 U.S.C. § 1330(b) (personal jurisdiction tied to subject-matter jurisdiction + proper service) and related service provisions in 28 U.S.C. § 1608; U.S. Const. amend. V (Due Process Clause) as the asserted constitutional overlay for personal jurisdiction.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that FSIA’s text supplies a complete personal-jurisdiction rule for suits against foreign states: if an FSIA immunity exception creates subject-matter jurisdiction and the foreign state is properly served under § 1608, § 1330(b) authorizes personal jurisdiction without any separate ‘minimum contacts’ showing. They contend that imposing an additional minimum-contacts requirement is inconsistent with the statutory design and foreign-relations sensitivities Congress addressed through FSIA’s comprehensive framework. Petitioners also argue that the doctrinal premise for minimum-contacts review is uncertain here because the Court has not decided whether foreign states are “persons” entitled to Fifth Amendment due-process protections, and lower-court reliance on dicta in Republic of Argentina v. Weltover has produced questionable reasoning and a split/instability in approach.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that, even in FSIA cases, constitutional due process limits federal-court assertions of personal jurisdiction, so plaintiffs must establish minimum contacts (typically with the United States as a whole under the Fifth Amendment) before haling a foreign sovereign (or its entities) into U.S. court. They emphasize that service and a statutory jurisdictional grant cannot override constitutional protections, and they rely on post-Weltover lower-court authority treating foreign states as not being ‘persons’ (or otherwise limiting jurisdiction), while also urging that this Court should deny review or decide narrowly because: (1) the Court has never resolved whether foreign states are Fifth Amendment “persons”; (2) the personal-jurisdiction analysis in this setting differs from the Fourteenth Amendment/state-court framework; (3) this case may involve an “agency or instrumentality” rather than the foreign state itself, raising distinct due-process questions; and (4) the Ninth Circuit did not fully resolve these issues in a way that would facilitate plenary Supreme Court review.
key_precedents: Republic of Argentina v. Weltover, Inc., 504 U.S. 607 (1992)
Price v. Socialist People’s Libyan Arab Jamahiriya, 294 F.3d 82 (D.C. Cir. 2002)
Frontera Resources Azerbaijan Corp. v. State Oil Co. of Azerbaijan Republic, 582 F.3d 393 (2d Cir. 2009)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains the constitutional one—that due process requires minimum contacts even if § 1330(b) says personal jurisdiction “shall exist.” But as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, that argument depends on a predicate this Court has not decided: whether a foreign state is a Fifth Amendment “person,” and Weltover merely assumed the point, so it cannot justify judicially grafting International Shoe onto Congress’s comprehensive FSIA scheme. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Price strengthens the case for restraint by underscoring the substantial doctrinal and historical doubt on the “personhood” premise; under judicial minimalism, we should decide the case on the statute’s text and leave any unavoidable constitutional question for another day. A narrow holding limited to suits against the foreign state itself—resting on § 1330(b)’s two conditions (FSIA exception + § 1608 service)—best preserves administrability and institutional legitimacy without foreclosing future consideration of agencies/instrumentalities or other contexts.

Textually, § 1330(b) supplies a complete rule—FSIA subject-matter jurisdiction plus § 1608 service—and under original public meaning I see no basis to graft an extra-textual contacts test onto that command. Justice Alito’s concern about undermining administrable uniformity in a foreign-relations statute reinforces, rather than displaces, the statutory and historical reasons to reject the respondent’s atextual overlay.

Justice Thomas’s invocation of Price reinforces that there is serious historical/doctrinal doubt about sovereign “personhood,” which means there is no clear constitutional command overriding the statute’s plain text. Given the FSIA’s calibrated foreign-relations framework and the practical costs of an amorphous, judge-made contacts overlay, I see no basis to depart from the statutory rule: FSIA exception plus § 1608 service suffices for personal jurisdiction over the foreign state itself.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument remains that the Fifth Amendment imposes an irreducible minimum-contacts limit even when § 1330(b) says personal jurisdiction “shall exist,” but that requires first establishing that a foreign state is a Fifth Amendment “person”—a premise Weltover expressly left undecided. Justice Kagan’s statutory-coherence point reinforces that Congress deliberately tied jurisdiction to narrow FSIA exceptions plus the demanding service safeguards of § 1608, and importing International Shoe would effectively reengineer that calibrated scheme in a sensitive foreign-relations area. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Price and the historical understanding that sovereigns are not the kind of “persons” due process was designed to protect in this posture further weakens any claim of a clear constitutional command. Absent a settled constitutional predicate, I’m not willing to constitutionalize an additional barrier that would predictably fall hardest on victims with no realistic alternative forum.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that the Fifth Amendment might impose a minimum-contacts backstop even if § 1330(b) says personal jurisdiction “shall exist,” but that argument is premature because it assumes—without a holding—that a foreign state is a due-process “person.” As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Weltover expressly only assumed that predicate, so it would be methodologically backwards to graft International Shoe onto a statute Congress drafted as a complete, administrable jurisdictional rule (FSIA exception + § 1608 service). Justice Thomas’s invocation of Price reinforces that the “personhood” premise is, at minimum, genuinely contested, which strengthens the case for deciding narrowly on statutory coherence rather than constitutionalizing an extra-textual overlay. Even if some residual fairness constraint ultimately exists, the FSIA’s calibrated exceptions and stringent service regime supply workable limits in this context without rewriting § 1330(b).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains constitutional: that due process independently requires minimum contacts even if § 1330(b) says personal jurisdiction “shall exist.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Weltover only “assum[ed], without deciding” that a foreign state is a Fifth Amendment “person,” so it cannot supply the clear constitutional premise needed to justify judicially grafting International Shoe onto a detailed statutory scheme. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Price further undercuts the claimed constitutional necessity by showing substantial doctrinal and historical support for the view that sovereigns are not due-process “persons.” Given the FSIA’s built-in procedural protections and the foreign-relations consequences of destabilizing Congress’s framework, I do not see a constitutional imperative strong enough to override the statute here.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1330(b) provides that, once an FSIA exception supplies subject-matter jurisdiction and the foreign state is properly served under § 1608, “personal jurisdiction” exists—Congress’s comprehensive scheme counsels against layering on an extra, judge-made minimum-contacts requirement absent clear constitutional necessity. This Court in Republic of Argentina v. Weltover expressly “assum[ed], without deciding” that a foreign state is a Fifth Amendment “person,” underscoring that the constitutional premise for minimum-contacts review here remains unresolved and that we should decide on narrower statutory grounds. Reading § 1330(b) as a complete personal-jurisdiction rule for foreign states also promotes uniformity and respects foreign-relations sensitivities that Congress addressed through the FSIA’s exclusive framework. Any due-process question about whether a foreign state (as distinct from an agency or instrumentality) is a “person” can be left for a case where it is unavoidable.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FSIA’s text supplies the rule for personal jurisdiction: 28 U.S.C. § 1330(b) provides that personal jurisdiction exists whenever a court has subject-matter jurisdiction under § 1330(a) (i.e., an FSIA immunity exception applies) and service is made under 28 U.S.C. § 1608; nothing in the statute adds a separate “minimum contacts” requirement. As an originalist and textualist, I would not graft onto this comprehensive jurisdictional scheme a judge-made due-process overlay absent clear constitutional command, particularly where this Court in Republic of Argentina v. Weltover, Inc. merely assumed “without deciding” that a foreign state is a Fifth Amendment “person.” Consistent with Price v. Socialist People’s Libyan Arab Jamahiriya, foreign states are not “persons” within the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, and thus no minimum-contacts showing is constitutionally required in suits against the sovereign itself. Because Congress expressly calibrated foreign-relations sensitivities through FSIA’s enumerated exceptions and service provisions, courts should enforce that enacted scheme as written rather than impose additional limits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1330(b) expressly provides that “[p]ersonal jurisdiction over a foreign state shall exist” for any claim within § 1330(a) where service is made under § 1608, and that text reads as a complete jurisdictional rule Congress enacted as part of the FSIA’s comprehensive framework governing suits against foreign sovereigns. Imposing an additional “minimum contacts” requirement not found in the statute undermines that design and injects uncertainty with serious practical consequences for enforcement of arbitral awards and other FSIA exceptions, where Congress chose a uniform federal standard keyed to immunity and service. Nor does existing precedent compel importing International Shoe into this setting, since the Court has not decided that a foreign state is a Fifth Amendment “person,” and lower-court reliance on Weltover’s dictum is too thin a basis to override § 1330(b)’s clear command. Given the FSIA’s foreign-relations sensitivities and Congress’s deliberate linkage of personal jurisdiction to subject-matter jurisdiction plus proper service, I would hold that no separate minimum-contacts showing is required for a “foreign state.”

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1330(b) of the FSIA makes personal jurisdiction in suits against a foreign state turn on two concrete requirements—subject-matter jurisdiction under an FSIA exception and proper service under § 1608—so layering an additional “minimum contacts” test would rewrite Congress’s comprehensive jurisdictional scheme and risk denying victims and other vulnerable plaintiffs a practical forum for relief. The asserted Fifth Amendment overlay is uncertain because this Court has strongly suggested in Republic of Argentina v. Weltover, Inc., 504 U.S. 607, 619 (1992), that foreign sovereigns, like States, are not “persons” entitled to Due Process Clause protections, undercutting the premise for constitutionally mandated minimum-contacts review. Even if due-process constraints apply in some form to agencies or instrumentalities, the foreign state itself is the defendant contemplated by § 1330(b), and Congress addressed fairness and foreign-relations concerns through narrowly drawn immunity exceptions and exacting service rules in § 1608 rather than through judge-made contacts tests. Given the real-world access-to-justice consequences, I would hold that a plaintiff need not separately prove minimum contacts once FSIA subject-matter jurisdiction and proper service are established.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: FSIA’s text sets out a comprehensive and workable personal-jurisdiction rule: under 28 U.S.C. § 1330(b), once an immunity exception supplies subject-matter jurisdiction and the foreign state is properly served under § 1608, “personal jurisdiction” follows, and layering on a separate minimum-contacts test risks undermining statutory coherence and Congress’s foreign-relations calibration. The constitutional overlay is uncertain because this Court has never decided whether a foreign state is a Fifth Amendment “person”; Weltover only “assum[ed] without deciding,” and the lower-court split (e.g., Price; Frontera) rests on contested premises. Given that uncertainty, and the statute’s clear jurisdictional mechanism tied to nationwide service and defined immunity exceptions, I would not constitutionalize an additional contacts requirement absent a clearer constitutional command. If due process applies at all here, FSIA’s built-in limits (narrow exceptions plus formal service) substantially address fairness and workability without importing the Fourteenth Amendment minimum-contacts framework.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1330(b) supplies the rule of decision for personal jurisdiction in FSIA suits: when an immunity exception yields subject-matter jurisdiction and service is made under § 1608, “personal jurisdiction over a foreign state shall exist,” leaving no textual room for an extra, judge-made “minimum contacts” overlay. Because Congress already balanced the foreign-relations sensitivities through FSIA’s immunity exceptions and strict service rules, courts should adhere to the statutory design rather than graft additional jurisdictional hurdles.

Weltover “assum[ed], without deciding” that a foreign state is a Fifth Amendment “person,” and longstanding interpretive principles suggest sovereigns are not “persons” for due-process purposes. Even if some due-process constraint applies, judicial restraint and practical workability favor adhering to the FSIA’s clear, administrable rule rather than importing unsettled minimum-contacts doctrine into this distinct federal/foreign-sovereign context. Given precedent, history, and the statute’s design, I would hold plaintiffs need not separately prove minimum contacts beyond § 1330(b) and proper § 1608 service.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FSIA’s text supplies a complete rule for personal jurisdiction over a “foreign state”: under 28 U.S.C. § 1330(b), once subject-matter jurisdiction exists under an FSIA exception and service is effected under § 1608, “personal jurisdiction over a foreign state shall exist,” leaving no textual room for an additional minimum-contacts overlay. case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal court may exercise personal jurisdiction over a foreign state (or its instrumentality) under the FSIA based solely on the statute’s jurisdiction/service provisions, or whether the plaintiff must also establish Fifth Amendment “minimum contacts” due process limits.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA), including its personal-jurisdiction/service framework (notably 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1608, 1603), and the U.S. Constitution’s Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause (and related doctrine stemming from International Shoe-style “minimum contacts”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that in FSIA cases plaintiffs should not be required to prove “minimum contacts” as a constitutional prerequisite to personal jurisdiction over a foreign sovereign. They contend that the FSIA already supplies the governing rule for personal jurisdiction (subject-matter jurisdiction under an FSIA exception plus proper service), and that treating foreign states as entitled to Due Process “minimum contacts” protection is doctrinally mistaken, historically unsupported, and harmful to U.S. foreign-relations and reciprocity interests. Petitioners also challenge lower-court reliance on post-Weltover dicta and structural arguments that foreign states are outside (or should be treated like U.S. States within) the constitutional ‘personhood’ framework.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the Court should deny review and, on the merits, that FSIA personal jurisdiction must still satisfy constitutional due process limits—i.e., a minimum-contacts showing—because foreign sovereign defendants (and at least their agencies/instrumentalities) are entitled to Due Process protections. They emphasize that the Court has never definitively decided whether foreign states are “persons” under the Fifth Amendment; that Weltover only assumed the point; and that the Ninth Circuit did not fully resolve key sub-issues (including whether an instrumentality has due process rights even if the sovereign does not). Respondents therefore maintain this case is a poor vehicle and that the Court should not reach broad constitutional questions unnecessarily.

Justice Kagan’s point about Weltover is decisive against respondent’s reliance on precedent: Weltover only “assumed, without deciding” foreign-state personhood, so it cannot constitutionalize a minimum-contacts overlay that displaces Congress’s comprehensive FSIA scheme. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh correctly emphasize that §1330(b) is written as a complete jurisdictional rule—FSIA subject-matter jurisdiction plus §1608 service—and constitutional avoidance cannot justify adding an atextual element that predictably frustrates the statute’s operation and Congress’s foreign-relations judgments. John Roberts.reasoning: The FSIA’s text makes personal jurisdiction turn on (1) subject-matter jurisdiction under an FSIA exception, 28 U.S.C. §1330(a), and (2) proper service under §1608, see §1330(b); adding an extra “minimum contacts” overlay is not a plausible construction but a judicial rewrite inconsistent with the statute’s comprehensive framework. Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FSIA’s text supplies the personal-jurisdiction rule: under 28 U.S.C. § 1330(b), personal jurisdiction exists where an FSIA immunity exception supplies subject-matter jurisdiction under § 1330(a) and service is made under § 1608; adding a free-floating Fifth Amendment “minimum contacts” overlay contradicts that statutory design. Even if Weltover assumed without deciding that a foreign state might be a “person,” that dicta should not be used to narrow remedial avenues for victims (often vulnerable plaintiffs) where Congress provided jurisdiction and notice protections through the FSIA’s service framework. On pragmatic grounds, requiring minimum contacts would create a substantial, often insurmountable barrier in precisely the cases where foreign sovereign conduct harms individuals and accountability depends on a federal forum.
